samples.prompt: Write a reflective narrative about revisiting a memory from your youth involving an unfinished or newly constructed building. Describe your philosophical impressions of the empty structure at the time and include a specific incident or action you took during your visit.
samples.generated:
I went back to the <PLACE> and found the new wing still under
construction. I walked round the walls and saw the men digging and
driving and pouring in the concrete. The great new towers were yet to be
painted and the whole place was a picture of the busy and almost
holy activity of human work. The only thing that I could say about it
then was that it seemed to me very like the new buildings which had been
put up for the last hundred years in <PLACE>. But the real truth is
that there was no such likeness at all. For when one looks at a modern
building one looks at it through a glass darkly; but when one walks round
the walls of <ORG>, one walks round them in the clear noonday.

The great tower has never been finished. The end of the world might come
and no man ever finish it. It may be finished by some unknown giant, and
it may be finished by my children. It may be finished before I die or
after I have died. But I can see the end of it now. I can see what it
would be like if the end came today. For the end of it would be like
<PLACE>; it would be beautiful, it would be eternal, it would be
incomparably more beautiful than anything I can find in <PLACE>.

In another part of the garden I met a boy with a box of matches.
He was putting out the fires in the old tower. But I do not think he put
out any fire worth putting out. He put out the matchbox.

samples.prompt: Write three short anecdotal examples illustrating how unconventional or eccentric behavior can be more persuasive than eloquent rhetoric.
samples.generated:
It is not necessary to go any further in this direction to show that
the ordinary methods of argument are far from being infallible. A man
may tell a story so vividly that men will believe him without his
having said anything at all. I have heard it said that Mr. <PERSON>
is a great debater. But I have also heard it said by his wife that he
was a great debater because he could make the most of an ass. A man may
tell a tale so simple and clear that it will make people think for
him. For instance, if a man were to say, “I am going to walk across
the world,” there would be some people who would take the thing very
seriously. There would be some people who would ask whether there was
a road, and what roads led where; there would be some people who would
ask him whether he had a mule. But if he began by saying, “I want to
be a mummy,” he need not trouble himself about roads, for the only road
that matters is the road of the dead. He would find all the roads that
mattered leading straight towards the place he wanted.

We have read of some celebrated philosopher who was so absent-minded
that he paid a call at his own house. My own absent-mindedness is
extreme, and my philosophy, of course, is the marvel of men and angels.
But I never quite managed to be so absent-minded as that. Some yards at
least from my own door, something vaguely familiar has always caught
my eye; and thus the joke has been spoiled. Of course I have quite
constantly walked into another man's house, thinking it was my own
house; my visits became almost monotonous. But walking into my own house
and thinking it was another man's house is a flight of poetic detachment
still beyond me. Something of the sensations that such an absent-minded
man must feel I really felt the other day; and very pleasant sensations
they were. The best parts of every proper romance are the first chapter
